The heart of this workflow is a two-file Quarto structure. Most tutorials use a single `.qmd` file for everything, but separating your analysis from your manuscript gives you the best of both worlds: a clean, readable paper and a fully transparent, reproducible analysis.

## Why two files?

| | `analysis.qmd` | `index.qmd` |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Reproducible analytical record | Clean journal manuscript |
| **Contains** | All R code, models, figures, tables | Prose, plus small hidden chunks that *display* precomputed figures/tables/stats |
| **Who reads it** | Reviewers, other researchers | Journal editors, readers |
| **Renders to** | HTML (best for code display) | PDF or Word for submission, HTML for a quick preview |
| **Tone** | Code-heavy, annotated | Academic prose |

Both files are version controlled together on GitHub. Together they give the complete picture of your research.

## How they connect

`analysis.qmd` runs all your R code and saves figures and derived data to the `outputs/` folder. `index.qmd` references those saved files.

```
analysis.qmd  →  runs R code  →  saves to outputs/figures/
                                                   ↓
index.qmd     →  references figure  →  manuscript PDF
```

This means:
- Changing your analysis in `analysis.qmd` automatically updates the figures, tables, and any inline numbers in `index.qmd` when you re-render
- Your manuscript stays clean — no *modelling or cleaning* code in the middle of your methods section
- A reviewer can open `analysis.qmd` and see every modelling decision you made

::: {.callout-note}
### A small exception: display-only chunks and inline code
"Text only" doesn't mean *zero* code in `index.qmd`. A tiny `echo: false` chunk that reads a saved table and prints it, or inline code like `` `r round(report_stats$mean_stone, 1)` `` in a sentence, is normal and encouraged — it's not analysis, just display. This is what keeps the numbers in your prose in sync with your actual results instead of a hardcoded value someone forgets to update after a revision.

**The rule of thumb:** any filtering, subsetting, or computation happens in `analysis.qmd` and gets saved to `outputs/`. `index.qmd` only ever *reads* — it never filters a data frame or picks out a row itself. If `index.qmd` needs `mean_stone`, `analysis.qmd` computes and saves `mean_stone`; `index.qmd` just loads it.
:::

## Structure of analysis.qmd

````{.quarto}
---
title: "Analysis: Kōura habitat preference study"
format: html
execute:
  echo: true        # show all code
  warning: false
  message: false
---

## Setup

```{{r}}
#| label: setup
# Packages are installed once via renv::restore() (see chapter 1) —
# no install.packages() here, so everyone gets the exact locked versions.
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

# Load raw data — never modify data/raw/ itself, only read from it
data <- read_csv("data/raw/koura_data.csv")
```

## Data cleaning

```{{r}}
#| label: data-cleaning

# Remove incomplete observations
data_clean <- data |>
  filter(!is.na(shelter_type)) |>
  mutate(size_class = cut(carapace_length_mm, 
                          breaks = c(0, 20, 35, Inf),
                          labels = c("juvenile", "sub-adult", "adult")))

# Save derived data
write_csv(data_clean, "data/derived/koura_clean.csv")
```

## Summary table

```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Mean carapace length by shelter type"

summary_table <- data_clean |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_length = mean(carapace_length_mm),
    sd_length = sd(carapace_length_mm),
    .by = shelter_type
  )

write_csv(summary_table, "outputs/tables/summary_table.csv")
summary_table
```

## Statistical models

```{{r}}
#| label: model-preference
#| cache: true

model_preference <- lm(carapace_length_mm ~ shelter_type, data = data_clean)
summary(model_preference)

saveRDS(model_preference, "outputs/model_preference.rds")

# Save exactly the values index.qmd needs to report inline. Computed and
# filtered here, in the reproducible record — index.qmd only ever reads
# this back, it never filters or subsets anything itself.
report_stats <- list(
  mean_stone = summary_table$mean_length[summary_table$shelter_type == "stone"],
  pvalue = summary(model_preference)$coefficients[2, "Pr(>|t|)"]
)
saveRDS(report_stats, "outputs/report_stats.rds")
```

## Figures

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-preference
#| fig-cap: "Kōura shelter preference by size class"

fig_preference <- ggplot(data_clean, 
                         aes(x = shelter_type, 
                             fill = size_class)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2E7D6B", "#4CAF93", "#A8D5C8")) +
  labs(x = "Shelter type", 
       y = "Count",
       fill = "Size class") +
  theme_minimal()

# Save for use in manuscript
ggsave("outputs/figures/fig-preference.png", 
       fig_preference, 
       width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)

fig_preference
```
````

::: {.callout-tip}
### Use `#| cache: true` for slow models
Some models take a while to run, especially with large datasets. Adding `#| cache: true` to those chunks means Quarto saves the result and skips re-running on the next render unless the code changes. Combined with `saveRDS()`, this keeps your workflow fast even as your analysis grows.
:::

## Structure of index.qmd

````{.markdown}

author: "Olivier V. Raven, A. N. Other"
date: today
format:
  pdf:
    documentclass: article
    linestretch: 2
  docx:
    reference-doc: journal-template.docx
  html:                          # handy for a quick preview, not for submission
    toc: true
bibliography: references/references.bib
csl: references/aquatic-conservation.csl
---

```{{r}}
#| label: setup-results
#| echo: false

library(tidyverse)
summary_table <- read_csv("outputs/tables/summary_table.csv")
report_stats <- readRDS("outputs/report_stats.rds")
```

Kōura showed a strong preference for stone configurations
over wood (see @fig-preference). Carapace length also differed
significantly by shelter type (mean stone = `r round(report_stats$mean_stone, 1)` mm,

````

::: {.callout-tip}
### Going further: rich scholarly metadata
The `author:` field can hold far more than a name — structured entries with ORCID iDs, affiliations, a corresponding-author flag, funding statements, and keywords, all of which flow through into your rendered PDF/HTML and are readable by indexers like Crossref. Handy for a thesis chapter or anything with multiple co-authors:

```yaml
author:
  - name:
      given: A. N.
      family: Other
    orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0000
    affiliations:
      - name: Your University
        department: Your Department
    corresponding: true
  - name:
      given: Second
      family: Author
    orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0001
    affiliations:
      - name: Collaborating Institution

keywords:
  - your keyword
  - another keyword

funding: "This research was supported by [funder], grant [number]."
```

See [Quarto's author/affiliations docs](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/front-matter.html) for the full schema.
:::

## Rendering both files

In Positron, you can render each file independently:

- Click **Render** in the top bar when `analysis.qmd` is open → generates HTML with all your code and outputs
- Click **Render** when `index.qmd` is open → generates your PDF manuscript

**Always render `analysis.qmd` first** if you have changed any code, so the figures in `outputs/figures/` are up to date before the manuscript renders.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Why does index.qmd load tidyverse and re-read the CSV again?
Each `.qmd` file renders in its own independent R session — `index.qmd` never sees the objects `analysis.qmd` created in memory, only the files it saved (`outputs/tables/summary_table.csv`, `outputs/report_stats.rds`, `outputs/figures/fig-preference.png`). That's the whole point of the two-file split: `index.qmd`'s hidden setup chunk just re-loads those saved results, it doesn't repeat any analysis.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
### Placeholder data example
The code examples on this page use realistic but placeholder kōura data. The actual data structure used in published kōura mesocosm studies includes columns for `shelter_type`, `carapace_length_mm`, `tank_id`, `round`, and `sex`. If you are adapting this for your own species, adjust the variable names accordingly.
:::

## Session info and reproducibility

At the end of your `analysis.qmd`, always include:

```r
#| label: session-info
sessionInfo()
```

This prints all package versions in your rendered HTML — a second line of defence alongside `renv.lock` for anyone trying to reproduce your work.
